props.title: The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes

sections.content: Disney's foray into technology-themed comedies kicked off with The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes, starring Kurt Russell as Dexter Riley, a college student who becomes a human computer after an electrical accident. This film launched a trilogy of Medfield College movies that captured late 1960s anxiety about computers while maintaining Disney's signature lightweight approach. The movie shares DNA with other technology-gone-wrong comedies like Weird Science (1985) and Short Circuit (1986), though with a distinctly family-friendly spin. Russell's charismatic performance helped establish his transition from Disney child star to leading man.

sections.content: The film reflects the era's simultaneous fascination with and fear of emerging computer technology. While primitive by today's standards, the computer effects and concepts mirror similar themes in later films like WarGames (1983) and Electric Dreams (1984). The movie's success spawned a 1995 remake starring Kirk Cameron, though it failed to capture the charm of the original. This brand of science-themed Disney comedy would continue through the 1970s with films like The Shaggy D.A. (1976) and The Cat from Outer Space (1978).

Director Robert Butler, who would later helm Hot Lead and Cold Feet (1978), brings a light touch to what could have been heavy-handed material about technology's impact on humanity. The film's Medfield College setting became a recurring location in Disney films, appearing in The Absent-Minded Professor (1961) and its sequel Son of Flubber (1963). These campus comedies established a formula Disney would return to repeatedly through the 1960s and 70s. SUBHEAD: The Disney Science Comedy Legacy

sections.content: The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes sits at an interesting intersection between Disney's earlier science comedies like The Absent-Minded Professor (1961) and their later tech-focused films like TRON (1982). The movie's blend of slapstick humor and mild sci-fi elements created a template that Disney would continue to mine in films like Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989) and Sky High (2005).
